tSNR across days and echoes

Benjamin Meyer

04 September 2026

Read the data

The file is comma-separated: column 1 is the subject ID, the remaining columns are tSNR values named r<run>e<echo> (R = resting-state scan, E = echo). NaN entries (runs/echoes missing for a subject) are read as NA.

tsnr <- read.csv(
  "tSNR_results.txt",
  header     = TRUE,
  na.strings = c("NA", "NaN", "")
)

names(tsnr)[1] <- "ID"
value_cols <- setdiff(names(tsnr), "ID")

str(tsnr)

Reshape to long format

run and echo are pulled out of the column names.

tsnr_long <- tsnr |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = all_of(value_cols),
    names_to  = "scan",
    values_to = "tSNR"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    scan = factor(scan, levels = value_cols),
    run  = as.integer(sub("^r(\\d+)e\\d+$", "\\1", scan)),
    echo = factor(as.integer(sub("^r\\d+e(\\d+)$", "\\1", scan)))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(tSNR))

head(tsnr_long)

Restrict to runs 1, 2 and 6, relabelled as days

Runs 1, 2 and 6 are the first resting-state scan of each of the three acquisition days. The mapping is taken from the acquisition loop in eeg_fmri_ext_SNR_2.sh (ses-Day1_task-rest1, ses-Day2_task-rest2, ses-Day3_task-rest6), and the EEG status from eeg_fmri_ext_SNR_1.m (“restscans 1, 6: without EEG; 2, 3, 4, 5: with EEG”):

Run Session Label here EEG
1 ses-Day1_task-rest1 Day 1 no
2 ses-Day2_task-rest2 Day 2 yes
6 ses-Day3_task-rest6 Day 3 no 
runs_keep <- c(1, 2, 6)
day_labels <- c("Day 1", "Day 2", "Day 3")

tsnr_day <- tsnr_long |>
  filter(run %in% runs_keep) |>
  mutate(
    day  = factor(run, levels = runs_keep, labels = day_labels),
    scan = droplevels(scan),
    echo = droplevels(echo)
  )

# The ANOVA is a fully within-subject design, so it needs subjects with a value
# in every day x echo cell.
n_cells <- length(runs_keep) * nlevels(tsnr_day$echo)

tsnr_rm <- tsnr_day |>
  group_by(ID) |>
  filter(dplyr::n() == n_cells) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(ID = factor(ID))

cat(
  "Complete cases: ", n_distinct(tsnr_rm$ID), " of ",
  n_distinct(tsnr_day$ID), " subjects\n", sep = ""
)
## Complete cases: 21 of 25 subjects

Subjects excluded, and which of the three runs they have:

tsnr_day |>
  group_by(ID) |>
  filter(dplyr::n() < n_cells) |>
  summarise(runs_present = paste(sort(unique(run)), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop")

Summary statistics

tsnr_rm |>
  group_by(echo, day) |>
  summarise(
    n      = dplyr::n(),
    mean   = mean(tSNR),
    sd     = sd(tSNR),
    median = median(tSNR),
    IQR    = IQR(tSNR),
    min    = min(tSNR),
    max    = max(tSNR),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(across(mean:max, ~ round(.x, 2)))

Plot

Black boxes and points, no background grid, explicit x- and y-axis lines, and base_size = 14 so the figure stays legible at A4 width. The x-axis is two-tiered: echo number on the axis itself, day beneath.

base_font <- 14   # readable when the 8 x 5.5 in figure is placed on A4

theme_tsnr <- theme_classic(base_size = base_font) +
  theme(
    panel.grid       = element_blank(),
    axis.line        = element_line(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    axis.ticks       = element_line(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5),
    axis.text        = element_text(colour = "black"),
    axis.title       = element_text(colour = "black"),
    axis.title.x     = element_text(margin = margin(t = 30)),
    axis.title.y     = element_text(margin = margin(r = 8)),
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = base_font + 1),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = base_font - 2),
    plot.caption     = element_text(size = base_font - 3, hjust = 0, colour = "grey30"),
    plot.margin      = margin(6, 8, 14, 6)
  )

theme_set(theme_tsnr)
n_echo <- nlevels(tsnr_rm$echo)

# One label per day, centred under that day's block of echoes.
day_tier <- data.frame(
  x     = seq_len(length(runs_keep)) * n_echo - (n_echo - 1) / 2,
  label = day_labels
)

# Jitter is horizontal only, so no point is drawn at a false tSNR value.
set.seed(42)

p_tsnr <- ggplot(tsnr_rm, aes(x = scan, y = tSNR)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "white", colour = "black",
    linewidth = 0.5, width = 0.62,
    outlier.shape = NA          # outliers are already shown as points below
  ) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.16, height = 0, seed = 42),
    shape = 21, fill = "black", colour = "white",
    size = 2.1, stroke = 0.35, alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = day_tier, aes(x = x, y = -Inf, label = label),
    vjust = 3.5, size = base_font / .pt, colour = "black",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(z) sub("^r\\d+e", "", z)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.04, 0.06))) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(
    title    = "Temporal SNR by echo and acquisition day",
    subtitle = "Each dot is one subject; Day 2 is the session acquired with EEG",
    x        = "Echo",
    y        = "tSNR (grey matter)",
    caption  = paste0("n = ", n_distinct(tsnr_rm$ID), " subjects with complete data")
  )

p_tsnr

Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA

Every subject contributes a value in all 12 cells, so day (3 levels) and echo (4 levels) are both within-subject factors. One ANOVA, with both main effects and their interaction. Greenhouse-Geisser is applied automatically where Mauchly’s test indicates a sphericity violation; ges is generalised eta-squared.

fit <- anova_test(tsnr_rm, dv = tSNR, wid = ID, within = c(day, echo))

get_anova_table(fit, correction = "auto")

Sphericity:

fit$`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity`
fit$`Sphericity Corrections`

Marginal means

tsnr_rm |>
  group_by(day) |>
  summarise(mean = round(mean(tSNR), 2), sd = round(sd(tSNR), 2), .groups = "drop")
tsnr_rm |>
  group_by(echo) |>
  summarise(mean = round(mean(tSNR), 2), sd = round(sd(tSNR), 2), .groups = "drop")

Post-hoc comparisons

Paired t-tests between days, Holm-corrected. First collapsed across echoes (follow-up to the day main effect), then within each echo (follow-up to the interaction).

pairwise_t_test(tsnr_rm, tSNR ~ day, paired = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "holm") |>
  select(group1, group2, statistic, df, p, p.adj, p.adj.signif)
tsnr_rm |>
  group_by(echo) |>
  pairwise_t_test(tSNR ~ day, paired = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "holm") |>
  select(echo, group1, group2, statistic, df, p, p.adj, p.adj.signif)

Size of the day differences, per echo

The interaction is easier to read as a proportion, because tSNR itself differs by a factor of three across echoes.

tsnr_rm |>
  group_by(echo, day) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(tSNR), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = day, values_from = mean) |>
  mutate(
    `Day 2 vs Day 1 (%)` = 100 * (`Day 2` - `Day 1`) / `Day 1`,
    `Day 3 vs Day 1 (%)` = 100 * (`Day 3` - `Day 1`) / `Day 1`,
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))
  )

Is the interaction just a scaling effect?

An equal proportional change across echoes would still show up as an interaction in absolute units, since echo 1 has three times the tSNR of echo 4. Refitting on log(tSNR) turns proportional effects into additive ones, so if the interaction were purely a scaling artefact it would disappear here.

tsnr_rm |>
  mutate(log_tSNR = log(tSNR)) |>
  anova_test(dv = log_tSNR, wid = ID, within = c(day, echo)) |>
  get_anova_table(correction = "auto")

Summary of observed effects

Echo dominates. tSNR falls monotonically with echo number — 73.2 (echo 1), 48.8, 33.4, and 23.7 (echo 4) — a very large effect (F(1.07, 21.33) = 1991.2, p < .001, ges = 0.89). This is the expected T2* decay: later echoes have longer TE, so less signal remains while thermal noise stays roughly constant. It is a property of the sequence, not a data-quality finding.

No effect of day. Collapsed across echoes, mean tSNR is 44.8 (Day 1), 44.1 (Day 2) and 45.4 (Day 3): F(2, 40) = 0.42, p = 0.661, ges = 0.007. No pairwise comparison survives correction. Image quality is stable across the three sessions, which is the reassuring result for a multi-day design.

A small day × echo interaction. F(2.2, 44.05) = 3.12, p = 0.049, ges = 0.007. It is carried by echo 1, which loses about 3.6% of its tSNR on Day 2 (73.9 → 71.2) and recovers on Day 3 (74.5), while echoes 2–4 vary by roughly 2% and do not dip. The interaction survives the log transform, so it is not merely the consequence of echo 1 sitting on a larger scale. Day 2 is the EEG session, and an EEG cap plausibly costs signal in the shortest-TE echo first — but with p just under .05, ges = 0.007, and no surviving post-hoc contrast, this should be treated as a hint to check rather than an established effect. Runs 3–5 (also EEG, same day) are available and would be the natural test of whether the echo-1 dip is reproducible.

Practically: the design is safe to pool across days, and echo weighting for the multi-echo combination can use the same weights on each day.

Does averaging tSNR over voxels make sense?

Partly. What is being analysed here is one number per subject, run and echo: the mean of the voxelwise tSNR map inside that subject’s grey-matter mask (fslstats -k … -M in eeg_fmri_ext_SNR_2.sh:104). For the question actually being asked — is image quality stable across sessions, and how does it scale with echo? — that is the right summary. It is a single scalar per cell, so the repeated-measures ANOVA above is exactly the correct test, it has real power at n = 21, and restricting to grey matter already avoids the main artefact of whole-brain averaging (ventricles and edge voxels dragging the mean around).

The averaging does, however, hide the things most likely to matter:

  • tSNR is strongly spatially non-uniform. It is high in the cortex and low in orbitofrontal and inferior temporal regions, where susceptibility dropout is worst. A stable global mean is compatible with a real loss confined to those regions.
  • Losses that trade off spatially cancel. If the EEG cap costs tSNR near the electrodes (superficial, occipital and frontal cortex) while deeper voxels are unchanged, the global mean moves by very little — which may be exactly what the small echo-1 effect is.
  • The mean is not where the optimal echo weighting lives. Optimal T2* weighting is voxelwise, since T2* varies regionally; a global mean per echo cannot inform it.

Does a voxel-wise analysis make sense?

Yes, and it is worth doing as a complement rather than a replacement — the maps already exist (*_bold_tSNR_masked.nii.gz), so the marginal cost is low. It answers the question the global mean cannot: where does tSNR change. The sensible route is to normalise each subject’s tSNR maps to a common template, then fit the same day × echo model voxelwise (SPM flexible factorial, or FSL randomise for a non-parametric test), with cluster- or TFCE-based correction for multiple comparisons.

Two things to plan for. First, the multiple-comparison penalty is real: a whole-brain voxelwise test of the ~2% day effect seen here will very likely find nothing, because the effect is small and diffuse rather than focal. Second, tSNR maps are smooth and heavy-tailed, so a non-parametric or log-transformed test is safer than assuming normality per voxel.

Given that, the most informative middle path is probably neither extreme: keep the global GM mean as the omnibus quality check, and add a small set of a priori ROI means — an occipital/electrode-adjacent ROI, a dropout-prone orbitofrontal ROI, and a deep/central ROI — analysed with the same day × echo model. That directly tests the EEG-proximity hypothesis suggested by the echo-1 dip, at a fraction of the correction burden of a whole-brain search. A full voxelwise map is then best used descriptively, to show the spatial distribution of tSNR per echo, rather than as the inferential test.
